subtitle: Sweet shell-topped buns
verso: Time for a little coffee: a concha and a little break.
story: The best-known pan dulce: a soft, slightly sweet bun under a crunchy sugar topping scored like a seashell. Picked up warm from the bakery with tongs and a tray, and eaten with coffee or hot chocolate.

ingredients.title: Dough
items: 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose or bread flour
¾ cup (180 ml) warm whole milk
6 tbsp (85 g) soft butter, plus a little melted butter for brushing

ingredients.title: Topping
items: ⅓ cup (65 g) vegetable shortening; butter works but spreads and blurs the shell

steps: Mix the flour, sugar, yeast and salt in a large bowl or stand mixer. Add the milk, eggs and vanilla and mix into a shaggy dough.
Knead 8–10 minutes (or with the dough hook on medium) until smooth. Add the butter a spoon at a time, kneading until each piece disappears. The dough should be soft, a little tacky and stretchy.
Cover and let rise in a warm place 1½–2 hours, until doubled.
Make the topping: mix the flour, powdered sugar, shortening and vanilla into a smooth paste like play dough. Divide into [[12 balls]].

Divide the dough into [[12 pieces]] (about 85 g each). Roll each into a smooth ball and set on parchment-lined sheet pans, 3 inches apart. Press each down slightly and brush with a little melted butter.
Flatten each topping ball between two pieces of plastic into a 3½-inch disc. Lay it on a bun and press gently so it sticks.
Score the topping in a shell pattern with a concha cutter or a sharp knife: curved lines fanning out from one side. Cut only through the topping, not the dough.
Cover loosely and let rise 1 hour, until puffy. The topping will crack open along the lines.
Bake at 350°F for 18–20 minutes, until the bottoms are golden. The tops should stay pale.
Cool a few minutes and eat warm.
pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Bread needs the oven.
tips: Brushing the buns with butter before the topping goes on keeps it from sliding off.
Bakers make the topping 1:1:1 by weight: flour, powdered sugar and shortening. In humid weather, add a spoonful more flour so it doesn't slide.
If your kitchen is cold, let the dough rise in the oven with only the light on.
Conchas go stale fast. Freeze extras the same day and warm them 5 minutes in the oven.

variations.name: Pan de Muerto
variations.subtitle: Day of the Dead bread
variations.note: Made for the Day of the Dead altar in late October and early November. An orange-blossom sweet bread decorated with dough bones and a round skull, brushed with butter and rolled in sugar. The four bones in a cross point to the four directions; some say they are tears. In Oaxaca it's pan de yema with a little face on top.

items: Concha dough from the base, with these changes: add the zest of 2 oranges, 1 tbsp orange blossom water and, if you like, ½ tsp anise seed, ground; use ½ cup milk plus ¼ cup orange juice instead of ¾ cup milk

steps: Make the dough and let it rise as in the base, steps 1–3.
Set aside about a quarter of the dough. Divide the rest into 2 or 3 pieces and shape each into a smooth round loaf on a lined sheet pan.

With the reserved dough, roll ropes and press your fingers along them to make knobby bones. Lay 4 across each loaf in a cross, and set a small ball (the skull) in the center. Stick them on with a little beaten egg.
Let rise 1 hour, brush with beaten egg and bake at 350°F for 30–35 minutes, until deep golden.
While warm, brush all over with melted butter and roll or sprinkle with sugar.

variations.name: Conchas de Chocolate
variations.subtitle: Chocolate conchas
variations.note: Every bakery tray has white and chocolate side by side. Make half and half.

items: Topping from the base, with 2 tbsp of the flour replaced by cocoa powder

steps: Top, score, rise and bake as in the base.
